Vine (Doctrine)
VINE
n.
Old English wīn-related; Hebrew gephen (grape vine) and kērem (vineyard); Greek ampelos (vine). One of the most extensive biblical metaphors, governing Israel as the LORD’s vineyard (Isa 5; Ps 80) and Christ Himself as the True Vine (John 15).

📖 Biblical Definition

The vine is one of the most extensive and theologically loaded metaphors of biblical literature, governing the LORD’s relationship to Israel as His vineyard and supremely Christ’s identification of Himself as the True Vine. The OT vine-and-vineyard imagery is foundational. Isaiah 5:1-7, the Song of the Vineyard, is the keynote: the LORD planted a choice vineyard in a very fruitful hill, fenced it, gathered out the stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the midst, made a winepress—and looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes. The prophet’s explicit interpretation: for the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. Psalm 80:8-19 develops the same imagery: thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it; the prayer for restoration is for the LORD to visit this vine, and the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted. Hosea 10:1; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15, 17, 19; Isaiah 27:2-6; Joel 1; Micah 4:4—the vine-and-vineyard is one of the most pervasive OT figures for Israel. The supreme New Testament use is John 15:1-8, Christ’s great I AM-discourse on the True Vine: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, Christ as the True Vine: Israel was the LORD’s vineyard but failed to bring forth the looked-for fruit; Christ is now Himself the True Vine, in whom the saints abide and from whom they bear fruit. Second, the Father as the Husbandman: tending the vine, pruning (purging) the fruitful branches that they may bring forth more fruit, taking away the unfruitful branches. Third, the abiding: abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. The branch derives its life-and-fruitfulness from union with the Vine; severed from Him, it is withered and gathered for burning. Fourth, the comprehensive scope: the vine-and-branches teaching covers the whole Christian life—union with Christ, the Father’s providential pruning, fruit-bearing through abiding, the seriousness of the unfruitful branch’s removal, the discipline of staying near to the Vine across every season. The biblical vine-doctrine is therefore one of the most extensive in the Bible, from Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard through to John 15’s True Vine, with the saint’s present life of abiding in Christ as the substantive application.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines VINE as a slender, climbing, or trailing plant; particularly, the plant which produces grapes; in scripture, one of the most extensive metaphors—Israel as the LORD’s vineyard (Isa 5; Ps 80) and supremely Christ Himself as the True Vine (John 15) from whom the saints derive their life-and-fruitfulness through abiding union.

VINE, n. — A slender climbing or trailing plant; particularly, the plant which produces grapes. In scripture, one of the great biblical metaphors, with Israel as the LORD’s vineyard and Christ as the True Vine.

BRANCH, n. — A part shooting from the trunk or main body of a plant; in John 15, the saints as branches in the Vine that is Christ, bearing fruit through abiding union with Him.

📖 Key Scripture

John 15:1-2 — "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit."

John 15:4-5 — "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."

Isaiah 5:1-2 — "Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine..."

Psalm 80:8 — "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The vine-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the antinomian-grace tradition that has minimized the severity of John 15’s removal-of-unfruitful-branches and the Father’s pruning-of-fruitful-branches (treating these as merely metaphorical without operative force)—and on the other by the works-righteousness tradition that has misread the fruit-bearing as the believer’s own work apart from the abiding-in-Christ source.

expand to see more

The antinomian-grace tradition has often minimized the severity of John 15’s explicit warnings. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away; if a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned. These are sober warnings about the consequences of not-abiding, which the antinomian tradition has often softened into general encouragements toward growth. Christ’s teaching is sharper. The Vine-and-branches imagery presents the believer with both the promise of much fruit through abiding and the warning of withering, gathering, and burning for the branch that does not abide. The pruning of even fruitful branches (the Father’s painful providential cutting-back that the branch may bring forth more fruit) is itself a sober reality the believer should expect rather than reflexively resist. The recovery is the recovery of John 15’s full weight: glorious promise of fruit through abiding paired with sober warning against not-abiding, with the Father’s purging of even fruitful branches as the appointed means of greater fruit.

The opposite corruption is the works-righteousness tradition that has misread the fruit-bearing as the believer’s own work apart from the abiding-in-Christ source. The branch in John 15 bears fruit not by its own striving but by its abiding-union with the Vine; the life of the Vine flows through the branch and produces the fruit. Without me ye can do nothing Christ says explicitly. The believer who treats Christian fruit as the product of his own strenuous effort, with Christ as the example or aid rather than the abiding source, has reversed the John 15 grammar. The recovery is the recovery of the abiding-priority: the saint’s primary work is to abide in Christ; the fruit follows by the Vine’s life flowing through the abiding branch; striving to bear fruit apart from abiding is the very pattern Christ explicitly rules out. The biblical vine-doctrine holds both: the seriousness of John 15’s warnings (against the antinomian softening) and the priority of abiding-union over strenuous fruit-production (against the works-righteousness reversal). The fruit follows the abiding; the abiding is the saint’s primary discipline; the Father’s pruning is real and to be welcomed; the consequences of not-abiding are severe and not to be softened away.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gephen (vine) and kērem (vineyard); Greek ampelos (vine); the great biblical metaphor of Israel as the LORD’s vineyard (Isa 5; Ps 80) culminating in Christ as the True Vine (John 15) from whom the saints derive life-and-fruitfulness through abiding union, with the Father as the Husbandman who prunes the fruitful and removes the unfruitful.

Hebrew gephen (H1612) — vine (over 50 OT uses).

Hebrew kērem (H3754) — vineyard (over 90 OT uses).

Greek ampelos (G288) — vine (John 15:1-5; Matt 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 22:18; Rev 14:18-19).

Greek ampelōn (G290) — vineyard (used in Christ’s vineyard parables, especially Matt 20-21).

Usage

"I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman—Christ’s great I AM-discourse on the union-with-Him from which fruit-bearing flows."

"Without me ye can do nothing—the abiding-union with Christ is the source; striving for fruit apart from abiding reverses the John 15 grammar."

"Antinomian softening misses the seriousness of John 15’s warnings; works-righteousness reversal misses the abiding-priority; biblical vine-doctrine holds both with full weight."
